<STATEMENT>
# Problem A — Zone Distribution

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

A cloud application runs across three availability zones labeled 1, 2, 3. There are n microservices. Some pairs of microservices provide redundant backups for each other and must not be placed in the same availability zone to prevent simultaneous failures. Assign every microservice to exactly one of the three availability zones so that no redundant pair shares a zone, or report that it is impossible.

## Input
The first line contains two integers n and m — the number of microservices and the number of redundant pairs (1 ≤ n ≤ 40, 0 ≤ m ≤ n·(n−1)/2).
Each of the next m lines contains two integers u v — a redundant pair.

## Output
If no valid assignment exists, print a single line NO.
Otherwise print YES on the first line. On the second line print n integers z₁ z₂ … zₙ (each in {1,2,3}), where zᵢ is the availability zone of microservice i. Among all valid assignments output the lexicographically smallest sequence (compare z₁ first, then z₂, and so on).

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
1 4
2 4
```
Output:
```
YES
1 2 3 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
4 6
1 2
1 3
1 4
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
NO
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
I replaced the "workers and shifts" framing with "microservices and availability zones" to provide a realistic cloud deployment scenario. The details added are: 1) "three availability zones" defines the data available for assignment; 2) "microservices" defines the items being assigned; 3) "redundant backups... must not be placed in the same availability zone" specifies the mutual exclusion constraint; 4) "Assign every microservice..." clarifies the exact objective. This minimal edit forces solvers to map redundancy constraints to graph coloring without relying on the word "conflict".
</RATIONALE>

The problem still requires partitioning n items into 3 sets such that specified pairs are separated, with the exact same lexicographical tie-breaking, ensuring identical outputs for all inputs.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>

The problem remains exactly Vertex 3-Coloring, which is NP-complete, with no structural changes to the graph or constraints.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
